2. Exploratory Data Analysis

Cancer is one of the leading causes of death in the U.S.. However due to the complexity of this condition, more research is needed to understand prevention, detection, and treatment. Our group chose to explore the data set “Cancer Risk Factors” created by Tarek Masryo to determine what lifestyle, environmental, and genetic factors influence five common cancer types. Findings from this research can provide insight on how these factors influence the diagnosis of the five common cancer types and possible actions people can take to prevent diagnosis.

This dataset has 2,000 observations of individual patients and 21 variables. Of the 21 variables, 2 are character (patient ID, cancer type), 2 are numerical (age, BMI), 4 are binary (gender, family history, BRCA mutation, H. pylori infection), and 13 are ordinal (smoking, alcohol use, obesity, diet red meat, diet salted processed, fruit vegetable intake, physical activity, physical activity level, air pollution, occupational hazards, calcium intake, risk level, overall risk score).

Cancer_Data %>% group_by (Cancer_Type) %>%
summarise(
  min_age = min(Age),
  max_age = max(Age),
  mean_age = mean(Age), 
  min_bmi = min(BMI),
  max_bmi = max(BMI),
  mean_bmi = mean(BMI))

3. Hypothesis Testing: Testing a Null Statistic

For the hypothesis testing, I chose to focus on a type of cancer that I believed would be easier to categorize with the variable age. The cancer chosen was Lung cancer. According to the American Cancer Society, apart from being the second most common cancer among both men and women, the average age of a lung cancer diagnosis is 70 years old, which is why I assigned the age variable to be 70.

Cancer_Data <- RKaggle::get_dataset("tarekmasryo/cancer-risk-factors-dataset")
Rows: 2000 Columns: 21

dbl (18): Age, Gender, Smoking, Alcohol_Use, Obesity, Family_History, Diet_R...

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
population_age <- 70

For the categories I chose to take from, the options I believed would relate best for Lung cancer were Age, air pollution, and overall risk score among other things.

Lung_Cancer <- Cancer_Data %>%
  filter(Cancer_Type == "Lung") %>%
  select(Age,Patient_ID, Gender, Smoking, Air_Pollution, BMI, Overall_Risk_Score)

Next I used my code to create four statistics around Lung cancer which were the sample size I would be taking from (527), mean age (61.22), median age (62), and standard deviation (9.67) all rounded to two decimal points. With these statistics I was able to develop evidence of the age of diagnosed lung cancer being relatively close to 70.

sample_size <- nrow (Lung_Cancer)
sample_mean <- mean (Lung_Cancer$Age)
sample_median <- median (Lung_Cancer$Age)
sample_sd <- sd (Lung_Cancer$Age)

print("Sample Statistics", quote= FALSE)
[1] Sample Statistics
print(sample_size)
[1] 527
print( round(sample_mean, 2))
[1] 61.22
print(round(sample_median, 2))
[1] 62
print(round(sample_sd, 2))
[1] 9.67

Next I created I bootstrap hypothesis test so I would be able to compare my mean age calculated from the sample to the mean age of the population. I set the seed at 475 to get the same number of samples every time the code is run. I picked 10,000 bootstrap samples so my p-value would be as accurate as possible and then I tested the null hypothesis by calculating the mean in comparison to the null distribution.

set.seed(475)
n_bootstraps <- 10000
null_distribution <- Lung_Cancer %>%
  specify(response = Age) %>%
  hypothesize (null = "point", mu = population_age) %>%
  generate(reps = n_bootstraps, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat= "mean")

p_val <- null_distribution %>%
  get_p_value(obs_stat = sample_mean, direction = "two-sided")
Warning: Please be cautious in reporting a p-value of 0. This result is an approximation
based on the number of `reps` chosen in the `generate()` step.
ℹ See `get_p_value()` (`?infer::get_p_value()`) for more information.
bootstrap_se <- sd(null_distribution$stat)
score <- (sample_mean - population_age) / bootstrap_se

print("Test Results", quote= FALSE)
[1] Test Results
print (round(sample_mean, 2))
[1] 61.22
print(population_age)
[1] 70
print(round(p_val$p_value,4))
[1] 0

From the bootstrap hypothesis I wanted to take the p-value that was calculated and have my code decide if I could reject or fail to reject the null. If the number calculated was less then 0.05 my code would assign it to reject the null hypothesis . If it was greater than 0.05 the code would fail to reject. I got a significantly low number >0.05 so the null was rejected.

if (p_val$p_value < 0.05) {
  print( "Reject the null hypothesis")
} else {
  print("Fail to reject", quote = FALSE)
}
[1] "Reject the null hypothesis"

Lastly I graphed my bootstrap values and the sample/population ages as a visual for why the data is significant. The mean age for the lung cancer data is much lower than the predicted average age of 70.

ggplot (null_distribution, aes(x= stat)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#003A5D", color = "white", bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sample_mean, color = "red", linewidth = 1)+
  labs(
    title = "Mean Age of Lung Cancer" ,
    x = "Mean Age",
    caption = "With Two Tails"
  ) + 
  theme_minimal()

4. Hypothesis Testing: Permutation Test

For the hypothesis testing, we looked for significant risk factors for colon cancer. Two diets were chosen, one red-meat and one high in salt and other processed foods. For the permutation test, it started off by loading in the data and then creating a High vs Low red-meat diet grouping based on the median value of Diet_Red_Meat. Then, we created a Colon Cancer (1/0) indicator and calculated the observed difference in colon cancer rates between the two diet groups of high and low. Next, we generated a null distribution by permuting the diet labels 5,000 times and computed a p-value to test whether the observed difference could be due to chance. Finally, we generated 5,000 bootstrap samples, calculated the bootstrap difference in proportions, and created a 95% bootstrap confidence interval and visualization of the bootstrap distribution.

# Pick one treatment effect: explanatory: diet_red_meat(yes/no), response: colon cancer(1/0).

# Find the median of diet_red_meat
cutoff <- median(Cancer_Data$Diet_Red_Meat, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 2: Create a new empty group column
Cancer_Data$Red_Meat_Group <- NA

# High red meat diet (>= median)
Cancer_Data$Red_Meat_Group[Cancer_Data$Diet_Red_Meat >= cutoff] <- "High"

# Low red meat in diet (< median)
Cancer_Data$Red_Meat_Group[Cancer_Data$Diet_Red_Meat < cutoff] <- "Low"

# Make sure it's treated as a categorical variable
Cancer_Data$Red_Meat_Group <- factor(Cancer_Data$Red_Meat_Group)

# Make sure cancer is numeric
Cancer_Data$ColonCancer <- ifelse(Cancer_Data$Cancer_Type == "Colon", 1, 0)
Cancer_Data$ColonCancer <- as.numeric(Cancer_Data$ColonCancer)

observed_stat <- Cancer_Data %>%
  group_by(Red_Meat_Group) %>%
  summarize(p = mean(ColonCancer)) %>%

observed_stat
[1] 0.3666667
# Create a null distribution 

set.seed(1)

perm_diffs <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled <- sample(Cancer_Data$Red_Meat_Group)
  
  Cancer_Data %>%
    mutate(Diet_Red_Meat_perm = shuffled) %>%
    group_by(Diet_Red_Meat_perm) %>%
    summarize(p = mean(ColonCancer)) %>%
    summarize(diff = p[Diet_Red_Meat_perm=="High"] -
                p[Diet_Red_Meat_perm=="Low"]) %>%
    pull(diff)
})

With these results, the extremely small p-value and a 95% bootstrap CI of [0.339, 0.395]—which does not include 0—provide strong evidence of a real relationship between higher red-meat consumption and increased colon cancer risk. Next, we repeated everything with the Diet_Salted_Processed and found that the p-value indicated statistical significance, and the 95% bootstrap CI of [0.119, 0.188]—which does not include 0—provides strong evidence of a real relationship between higher salted/processed food consumption and increased colon cancer risk.

5. Modeling Relationships (Correlation and Regression)

We wanted to model the relationship of Prostate Cancer and age to find the correlation and make a model for regression. We started by creating a binary variable, ProstateCancer, coded as 1 for “Prostate” and 0 otherwise, to allow numeric analysis. We then checked the structure and summary of Age to understand its distribution. A linear regression model was fitted predicting ProstateCancer from Age, and the coefficients were examined to assess the relationship. Finally, a scatter plot with a fitted regression line was generated to visualize the trend between age and prostate cancer risk.

Cancer_Data$ProstateCancer <- ifelse(Cancer_Data$Cancer_Type == "Prostate", 1, 0)
Cancer_Data$ProstateCancer <- as.numeric(Cancer_Data$ProstateCancer)

Next, we used bootstrap resampling to estimate the sampling distribution of the slope for ProstateCancer predicted by Age. We started by creating a seperate dataset that only had cancer data for males because Prostate Cancer onlu affects males. By generating 5,000 bootstrap samples and calculating the slope for each, we assessed the variability of the estimated relationship. A 95% bootstrap confidence interval was then computed, ranging from 0.0178 to 0.0228, indicating that the slope is consistently positive across resamples. The scatterplot shows that prostate cancer rate tends to increase slightly with age. The fitted regression line indicates a positive relationship. The confidence interval for the slope is very narrow and entirely above zero, supporting that the increase in age is significantly associated with a higher cancer rate.

cancer_males <- Cancer_Data %>% 
  filter(Gender == 1)

cancer_males$ProstateCancer <- ifelse(cancer_males$Cancer_Type == "Prostate", 1, 0)
cancer_males$ProstateCancer <- as.numeric(cancer_males$ProstateCancer)


model <- lm(ProstateCancer ~ Age, data = cancer_males)
summary(model)
